```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 4, warning = TRUE, message = TRUE)
library(NationalModelUng2009)
```

## What this workflow provides

This workflow predicts gross merchantable volume in cubic metres per hectare
(m3/ha) using the national models of Ung et al. (2009). Gross merchantable
volume is the volume of live trees larger than 9 cm in diameter at breast
height.

The example starts where many users start: a file of stand locations with
their leading species. It ends with one yield curve, from age 0 to 200, for
each species in each stand.

## 1. Read the stands

The package includes a small made-up file of 10 stands. Each stand has an
identifier, a location (latitude, longitude and elevation in metres) and up to
three leading species, written as short inventory codes. Most stands have one
species; two have two species and one has three.

```{r stands}
stands <- read.csv(
  system.file("extdata", "example_stands.csv", package = "NationalModelUng2009"),
  na.strings = ""
)
stands
```

## 2. One row per stand and species

Each species in a stand gets its own curve, because the models were fitted to
stands where one species made up most of the basal area. Stack the three
species columns into one, then drop the empty ones.

```{r stack}
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(stand_id = stands$stand_id, code = stands$sp1),
  data.frame(stand_id = stands$stand_id, code = stands$sp2),
  data.frame(stand_id = stands$stand_id, code = stands$sp3)
)
curves <- curves[!is.na(curves$code), ]
curves <- curves[order(curves$stand_id), ]
nrow(curves)
```

There are 15 curves to make.

## 3. Translate species codes into accepted names

The package accepts a species by its common name, scientific name or package
code. `ung_species()` lists them.

```{r species-list}
head(ung_species())
```

Inventory codes are not accepted, so make a small lookup table that gives the
common name for each code you use.

```{r species-lookup}
lookup <- data.frame(
  code = c("SB", "PJ", "BF", "RS", "BW", "PW", "PR", "PL", "HW", "FD", "AW"),
  species = c("black spruce", "jack pine", "balsam fir", "red spruce",
              "white birch", "eastern white pine", "red pine",
              "lodgepole pine", "western hemlock", "Douglas-fir",
              "trembling aspen")
)
curves$species <- lookup$species[match(curves$code, lookup$code)]

# Every code must have a name, and every name must be accepted
stopifnot(!anyNA(curves$species),
          all(curves$species %in% ung_species()$common))
```

## 4. Get the climate for each stand

The models need two climate values for each stand:

- `dd0`: degree-days above 0 °C (the yearly sum of daily mean temperatures
  above 0 °C);
- `map`: mean annual precipitation in millimetres.

Use **averages over a 30-year period** (climate normals, such as 1981–2010),
not the values of one year. The models were fitted with one long-term climate
for each plot. Those values describe where a stand grows, not the weather of
a given year. One unusual year would move the whole curve.

Two programs can provide these values. Both are run for 1981–2010 averages
below. They need a network connection or a local install, so the code is not
run here.

**Option A: climr (in R).** `ung_climate()` uses the climr package. climr
downloads climate maps the first time an area is requested (this can take
several minutes) and keeps them for later use. Some VPNs block its server; if
climr cannot connect, disconnect from the VPN or use Option B.

```{r climate-climr, eval = FALSE}
climate <- ung_climate(lon = stands$lon, lat = stands$lat,
                       elev = stands$elev, id = stands$stand_id)
```

**Option B: ClimateNA (Windows program).** The same function runs a local
copy of ClimateNA when you set `source = "climatena"` and give the path to
the program.

```{r climate-climatena, eval = FALSE}
climate <- ung_climate(lon = stands$lon, lat = stands$lat,
                       elev = stands$elev, id = stands$stand_id,
                       source = "climatena",
                       exe = "C:/ClimateNA_v760/ClimateNA_v7.60.exe")
```

For another period, give the years to average, for example
`years = 2010:2019`. This works with both options.

If you already have `dd0` and `map` from another source, skip this step and
add them to `curves` yourself. If you ran ClimateNA yourself, convert its
output with `ung_climate_from_climatena()`.

Neither program reports `dd0` directly. Both functions calculate it from
three other degree-day variables (see `?ung_climate`). Do not use ClimateNA's
`DD5` (degree-days above 5 °C) or `DD_0` (degree-days *below* 0 °C) as `dd0`.

The package includes the results of both options for the example stands.
This example uses the climr values.

```{r climate-example}
climate <- read.csv(
  system.file("extdata", "example_climate_climr.csv",
              package = "NationalModelUng2009")
)
# The ClimateNA values are in "example_climate_climatena.csv"
curves <- merge(curves, climate, by.x = "stand_id", by.y = "id")
curves
```

## 5. Make the yield tables

`ung_yield_table()` makes all the curves in one call. Give it one value of
`species`, `dd0` and `map` per curve, and the ages you want. The `id`
argument labels each curve, here with the stand identifier.

```{r yield-long}
ages <- seq(0, 200, by = 10)
yield <- ung_yield_table(curves$species, age = ages,
                         dd0 = curves$dd0, map = curves$map,
                         id = curves$stand_id)
head(yield)
```

The result is in long format: one row per curve and age, with columns `id`,
`species` (the package code, such as `PINU.BAN` for jack pine), `dd0`, `map`,
`age` and `volume`. Age 0 always has volume 0.

The default model is Nat2 (see "Which model to use" in `?ung_volume`).

The warning above is a single summary for the whole call. Here it says that
some curves go beyond the oldest stands in the data used to fit the models.
Step 7 shows which rows are affected.

CBM users may prefer the wide format, with one row per curve and one volume
column per age (`vol_0`, `vol_10`, ...). Add `format = "wide"` to the same
call.

```{r yield-wide}
yield_wide <- ung_yield_table(curves$species, age = ages,
                              dd0 = curves$dd0, map = curves$map,
                              id = curves$stand_id, format = "wide",
                              warn = FALSE)
yield_wide[, 1:8]
```

## 6. Add an uncertainty interval

Add `uncertainty = TRUE` to get `lower` and `upper` columns. They hold the
central 90 % interval of many simulated volumes. `seed` makes the random
simulation repeatable.

```{r yield-uncertainty}
yield_unc <- ung_yield_table(curves$species, age = ages,
                             dd0 = curves$dd0, map = curves$map,
                             id = curves$stand_id,
                             uncertainty = TRUE, seed = 1, warn = FALSE)
yield_unc[yield_unc$age == 100, c("id", "species", "volume", "lower", "upper")]
```

The interval includes two sources of uncertainty:

- **rounding of the published parameters**, which were published to four
  decimal places (the unrounded values are not available). Keep the default
  `rounding = TRUE`;
- **slightly different climate**. By default, `dd0` and `map` vary as much as
  they do across all the fitting plots for that species in Canada, so the
  interval is wide. If you know how uncertain your own climate values are,
  set `sd_dd0` and `sd_map`.

It does **not** include the uncertainty of the fitted parameters or the
variation of real stands around the model, so real stands vary more than the
interval shows. See `?ung_uncertainty` for details and a plot.

## 7. List all cautions with `ung_check()`

`ung_check()` runs every check the package knows about and explains how many
rows each one affects.

```{r checks}
ung_check(yield)
```

The first five checks are the kinds that can trigger the warning in step 5.
The others apply to almost every yield curve, so they are listed here rather
than given as warnings. `ung_check()` always calculates both Nat1 and Nat2,
so it can flag rows the warning did not mention: here, `output_beyond_data`
also counts Nat1 basal area. The limits of 10 years, 15 % and 30 % are rules
of thumb chosen for this package, not values from the paper.

To see which curves and ages are affected, use `rows = TRUE`.

```{r check-rows}
flags <- ung_check(yield, rows = TRUE)
old <- yield[flags$older_than_data, ]
table(old$id, old$species)
```

## 8. Plot the curves

`plot()` draws one line per curve. Here are the three black spruce stands.

```{r plot}
bs <- curves[curves$species == "black spruce", ]
plot(ung_curve(bs$species, age = ages, dd0 = bs$dd0, map = bs$map,
               warn = FALSE))
```

The two Douglas-fir stands show a weakness of Nat2 in dry places. At stand
S10, the Nat2 curve (dashed) reaches 85 m3/ha by age 10 and then rises
slowly, which is not realistic. This comes from the published Nat2 equation:
its climate terms control how fast volume rises with age. Nat1 (solid) rises
gradually, so consider Nat1 for such stands. With the slightly drier
ClimateNA climate for S10, the Nat2 curve is even flatter, and the warning
and `ung_check()` report it as `curve_not_rising`.

```{r plot-fd}
fd <- curves[curves$species == "Douglas-fir", ]
plot(ung_curve(fd$species, age = ages, dd0 = fd$dd0, map = fd$map,
               model = "both", nat1_bias_correction = TRUE, warn = FALSE))
```

## 9. Compare Nat1 and Nat2

Nat2 predicts volume directly. Nat1 first predicts dominant height and basal
area `G`, then calculates volume from them. The published Nat1 is biased low;
`nat1_bias_correction = TRUE` adds a correction that closes most of the gap
(see "Why Nat1 volume needs a correction" in `?ung_volume`). The correction
was added by this package and is not part of the published model.

```{r compare-models}
s02 <- curves[curves$stand_id == "S02", ]
both <- ung_curve(s02$species, age = ages, dd0 = s02$dd0, map = s02$map,
                  model = "both", warn = FALSE)
both_corrected <- ung_curve(s02$species, age = ages, dd0 = s02$dd0,
                            map = s02$map, model = "both",
                            nat1_bias_correction = TRUE, warn = FALSE)
data.frame(age = both$age,
           Nat1 = both$V_Nat1,
           Nat1_corrected = both_corrected$V_Nat1,
           Nat2 = both$V_Nat2)[both$age %in% c(40, 80, 120), ]
plot(both_corrected)
```

To use Nat1 in a yield table, add `model = "Nat1"` and, usually,
`nat1_bias_correction = TRUE` to `ung_yield_table()`.

## 10. Test climate sensitivity

`ung_sensitivity()` raises and lowers `dd0` and `map` by 100 and reports the
largest percentage change in volume. A large change means the curve depends
strongly on getting the climate right.

```{r sensitivity}
sens <- ung_sensitivity(curves$species, age = 80, dd0 = curves$dd0,
                        map = curves$map, model = "Nat2")
cbind(stand_id = curves$stand_id[sens$row],
      sens[, c("species", "volume", "max_change_pct")])
```

## 11. Save the yield tables

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
write.csv(yield, "yield_long.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(yield_wide, "yield_wide.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Limits of the models

- The authors designed these models for predictions over less than 10 years.
  A curve from age 0 to 200 goes far beyond that; treat it as an illustration
  of the fitted equations, not a forecast for a particular stand.
- The models were fitted to plots measured once, where one species made up at
  least 75 % of the basal area. In a mixed stand, each species' curve
  describes a stand of that species alone. Combining the curves (for example,
  weighting them by each species' share) is up to the user.
- The models have no site-quality input. Two stands with the same species
  and climate get the same curve.
- The climate terms describe how volume differs among locations. They do not
  predict the effect of climate change, so do not use future climate
  projections as inputs.

## Reference

Ung, C.-H., Bernier, P.Y., Guo, X.J. and Lambert, M.-C. 2009. A simple growth
and yield model for assessing changes in standing volume across Canada's
forests. The Forestry Chronicle 85(1): 57–64. <https://doi.org/10.5558/tfc85057-1>
